title: The state cereal system (Office des Céréales monopoly, decreed prices, CGC subsidies) built in 1962-1971 now strains public finances and blunts market signals

rootCauses.cause: Creation of the Office des Céréales in 1962 with control of grain trade, and annual decrees fixing producer and resale prices

Creation of the Caisse Générale de Compensation (1970 or 1971) to subsidise cereal products for all consumers; bread prices stay politically sensitive since the 1983-84 bread riots, and subsidy reform has been postponed so far
Subsidy needs rise with world grain prices and bad harvests, while budget transfers to the system do not keep pace

author: TahaGHZ
excerpt: Cereal marketing in Tunisia is run by state bodies created soon after independence. The Office des Céréales (OC) was created in 1962. It controls wheat imports and sells imported wheat at subsidised prices. Cereal…

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content: Cereal marketing in Tunisia is run by state bodies created soon after independence. The Office des Céréales (OC) was created in 1962 (SRC-TG-705, SRC-TG-706). It controls wheat imports and sells imported wheat at subsidised prices (SRC-TG-704). Cereal producer and resale prices are fixed by government decree each campaign (SRC-TG-711, SRC-TG-705). The Caisse Générale de Compensation (CGC) pays operators along the chain the gap between market and administered prices. Bread, pasta and couscous therefore reach consumers at subsidised prices (SRC-TG-705). Sources give 1970 (SRC-TG-705) and 1971 (SRC-TG-706) as the CGC's creation date. The system now costs the state large sums it does not pay on time. For 2022-2023 the OC was owed TND 6,625 million by the CGC but received only 38%. Its bank debt reached TND 6,343 million, 83% of it to the Banque Nationale Agricole, and its unaudited 2023 balance was TND -900 million (SRC-TG-705). The World Bank links OC's financing gap to its trouble securing imports: it finds it "very difficult" for the OC to get more bank financing for grain imports (SRC-TG-705). USDA and FAO report wheat and flour shortages in 2023/24 caused by weaker procurement capacity (SRC-TG-703, SRC-TG-700).

sections.heading: Root causes
sections.content:
**Past decisions.**

- 1962: decree-law 62-10 created the Office des céréales, légumineuses alimentaires et autres produits agricoles (SRC-TG-711). It was part of a state-led ("dirigiste") policy of public offices for each strategic commodity (SRC-TG-706). Over 1960-1970, producer prices of farm products were fixed and kept low (SRC-TG-706).
- 1970/71: the CGC was created to manage subsidies (SRC-TG-706, SRC-TG-705). After the structural adjustment of 1986 onwards, subsidies were cut for several products. Cereals for human consumption kept them (SRC-TG-706).
- The 1983-84 bread riots, set off by a bread price increase, are cited by the World Bank as a reason the subsidy remains politically sensitive (SRC-TG-705). USDA says bread subsidies have stayed unchanged despite the budget burden (SRC-TG-703). FAO says subsidy reform has been discussed but postponed (SRC-TG-700).

**How the system shapes incentives today.**

- *Producer side.* The sources disagree, and they describe different periods. The World Bank's 2014 review describes guaranteed cereal prices as market price support: cereals took about a third of market price support spending. That review found support skewed towards large wheat farms, because it is paid on output and farm size (SRC-TG-710). The World Bank's 2024 paper says OC farmgate prices "have been below import-parity prices". Even after increases of about 61-64% between 2021 and 2023, the February 2024 farmgate prices for durum and barley were 3% and 14% below OC import cost (SRC-TG-705). Whether producer prices act as a subsidy or a tax therefore depends on world prices in a given year. The decreed price is fixed for the whole season. The 2014 review also notes "inadequate quality bonuses" for cereals (SRC-TG-710).
- *Collection.* The sources disagree on whether the OC still controls collection. The World Bank says the OC has a de jure monopoly over domestic collection and imports (SRC-TG-705). USDA says collection has been privatised for both wheat and barley (SRC-TG-703). ITES reports that the OC's share of physical collection fell from 32% in 2005 to 2% in 2012, as private operators (58%) and SMSA cooperatives (40%) took over (SRC-TG-706). This does not mean the OC handles only 2% of the market. USDA says collection by the Cereal Board accounts for 40-60% of wheat production and 10-40% of barley (SRC-TG-703), and the OC collected 1,284.7 kt in 2019 (SRC-TG-705). Our reading, not stated by the sources, is that ITES counts only collection the OC performs with its own facilities, while private and cooperative collectors buy grain that then enters the OC system at decreed prices. The 2% figure should not be read as the OC's current market share. The firmer monopoly today is over wheat imports and the sale of wheat to millers (SRC-TG-704). Barley imports were opened to private firms in April 2023 (SRC-TG-705).
- *Consumer side.* Universal subsidies keep demand for bread wheat high and encourage waste and misuse. The World Bank reports 900,000 baguettes wasted daily, semolina used as animal feed and leakage across borders (SRC-TG-705). The World Bank gives no year for the baguette figure. ITES attributes the same 900,000 loaves a day to the Institut National de la Consommation (INC) and dates it 2017 in its 2035 scenario table (SRC-TG-706). A 2017 press report of INC data dates the estimate to 2014 (SRC-TG-906, tier C). The year therefore differs between sources. It is an older estimate repeated in later documents, not a 2024 measurement (see FND-TG-900). This feeds the import dependence in FND-TG-700. The subsidy is not well targeted. The World Bank's 2022 incidence analysis found 43.3% of the 'gros pain' bread subsidy goes to the poorest two quintiles (SRC-TG-705). An older INS 2013 analysis cited by ITES found only 9.2% of all food subsidies reached the poorest households in 2010 (SRC-TG-706, citing INS). These two figures measure different things and should not be compared directly.
- *Fiscal.* Food subsidies cost about 1.5% of GDP in 2009 and over 3% in 2012 (SRC-TG-710). The CGC's arrears to the OC are a symptom. The cause is that subsidy needs rise with world prices and bad harvests, while budget transfers do not keep pace (SRC-TG-705, SRC-TG-700).

sections.heading: Evidence
sections.content: See indicators. Key figures from the World Bank's March 2024 project paper (OC data, unaudited) are the arrears, the bank debt and the 2023 deficit (SRC-TG-705). Decree 2012-754 (prices for the 2011 harvest) shows the mechanism. It fixed base producer prices (43 TND/q durum, 35 TND/q soft wheat) and an intervention price for barley, along with resale prices to millers (SRC-TG-711). By 2023 producer prices had reached 1,300 TND/t for durum (130 TND/q) and 1,000 TND/t for soft wheat (SRC-TG-700, SRC-TG-704).

sections.heading: Why confidence is what it is
sections.content: Medium. The institutional facts (OC 1962, decreed prices, CGC payments, OC finances) rest on an official decree and on World Bank documents that use OC data. The OC figures are unaudited. The direction of the producer price incentive is contested between sources and periods. The current fiscal cost of the cereal subsidy is a data gap, because only press figures were found. The 2014 World Bank analysis rests on models from 2006-2009.

sections.heading: Links to other sectors
sections.content:
- Water: the state also subsidises irrigation water for wheat (USD 0.07/m3, 32% of cost) to raise output (SRC-TG-704). This is the same food-security logic of price support, applied to water.
- Energy: none found.

sections.heading: Leads for phase 2
sections.content:
- World Bank-supported grain value chain reform plan, nine measures. These include farmgate price increases, barley import liberalisation, an increase in OC barley sales prices, taxation of PS-7 pastry flour users, digital tracking of durum distribution, a 7% higher flour extraction rate and soft wheat import liberalisation for PS-7. Estimated savings are US$576 million a year (SRC-TG-705).
- Georeferenced inventory of bakeries, "classified" vs "modern" (December 2023) (SRC-TG-705)
- Food subsidy reform plan with a switch to cash transfers, in the project results framework (SRC-TG-705)
- ITES proposal to target subsidies by place of consumption (households vs out-of-home) (SRC-TG-706)
- Tunisia Emergency Food Security Response Project P179010 / P181565

sections.heading: Verification
sections.content: **Independent review, 21 November 2026:** pass after corrections. Checked against the originals: World Bank PAD5602 of 1 March 2024, paragraphs 9-10 and footnotes 3, 15 and 17 (SRC-TG-705); GIEWS briefs of 29 November 2023 and 18 February 2026 (SRC-TG-700); decree 2012-754, articles 1 and 7-10 (SRC-TG-711); World Bank Unfinished Revolution ch. 9, market price support and food subsidy paragraphs (SRC-TG-710); ITES collection section, 2035 scenario table and footnote 107 (SRC-TG-706); USDA GAIN TS2024-0003 marketing section (SRC-TG-703); Economiste Maghrebin, 25 May 2017 (SRC-TG-906). Corrections: the 900,000-loaves indicator and Consumer-side text now state that ITES dates the figure 2017 and the 2014 date comes only from the 2017 press report (SRC-TG-906, tier C). Reviewer objection that the large-farm skew mechanism ("paid on output and farm size") is absent from SRC-TG-710 was not confirmed: the chapter says "most support is provided based on output and farm size", so the text is unchanged. The two points the review left unchecked were reopened and confirmed: FAO (GIEWS) says subsidy reform "has been postponed so far", and decree 2012-754 article 8 fixes normal resale (retrocession) prices of the Office des Cereales. Independent teammate sign-off is outstanding; reviewer and author share the TahaGHZ identity, so the record is not validated.

resolvedSources.title: GIEWS Country Brief: The Republic of Tunisia (archive of briefs 2010-2026)
resolvedSources.publisher: FAO Global Information and Early Warning System (GIEWS)
resolvedSources.extracts:
Brief of 29 November 2023 (archive PDF, brief dated 29-November-2023):

> Cereal cultivation is mostly rainfed, resulting in significant year-on-year variations. The irrigated wheat area represents less than 15 percent of the total wheat planted area.

> Coupled with above-average temperatures during the critical crop development stages, severe drought conditions, not experienced in the country for over two decades, constrained crop development, leading to widespread crop failures. Consequently, 2023 cereal output was estimated at 302 000 tonnes, almost 80 percent below the average.

> In 2023, the guaranteed farmgate prices of durum wheat increased to TDD 1 300 (USD 436), up from TDD 1 000/tonne (USD 339). The guaranteed farmgate prices of soft (common) wheat increased from TDD 800 (USD 271) to TDD 1 000/tonne (USD 336) and those of barley from TDD 690 (USD 233) to TDD 800 (USD 267). In 2023, the government purchased 225 600 tonnes of grains, compared to 700 000 tonnes in 2022.

> Cereal import requirements in the 2023/24 marketing year (July/June) are forecast at 4.7 million tonnes, about 30 percent above the average import requirements of the previous year. More than half of the imported cereals is wheat.

> Between 2016 and 2020, the country sourced almost 40 percent of its wheat imports from Ukraine, 7 percent from the Russian Federation and the rest from various European Union countries.

> In spite of the country's high import dependency rate, changes in international prices of wheat products and vegetable oil are not fully transmitted into domestic prices as the government's universal food subsidy programme keeps them stable. There have been discussions about reforming the subsidy system, which puts a significant burden on the national budget, but the implementation has been postponed so far.

Brief of 30 May 2024:

> The aggregate 2023 cereal output, mainly wheat, is estimated at 520 000 tonnes, about 70 percent below the five-year average.

> The country relies heavily on grain imports, even in years with good domestic production, and cereals constitute the largest share of the value of imports.

> Imports cover more than half of the country's cereal consumption needs. Cereal imports in the 2023/24 marketing year (July/June) are forecast at 4 million tonnes and above the five-year average.

> Durum wheat for couscous and pasta, and soft wheat for bread, represent the main components of the local diet and account for around 45 percent of the food calorie intake.

> Four consecutive years of drought have weakened the seed production system and the 2022/23 harvest of durum wheat was not sufficient to guarantee seeds for the 2023/24 campaign. As a consequence, the government increased imports of wheat seed, while some farmers decided to shift to barley production.

> In the period between July 2023 and May 2024, the Russian Federation and Ukraine supplied about half of the wheat imports to the country, while about 30 percent was supplied by Bulgaria and Turkey.

> the rise of international food prices translated into increased value of subsidies leading to public debt growth and reduced the country's import capacity, causing shortages of basic food products such as wheat, coffee, tea and vegetable oils.

Brief of 27 July 2022:

> The country aims to reach an annual domestic production of 3 million tonnes of cereals to achieve self-sufficiency.

> In 2022, the average import prices of durum wheat so far reached USD 665/tonne, up from USD 435 in 2021 and USD 327 in 2020. Likewise, import prices paid for 1 tonne of soft (common) wheat increased from USD 231 in 2020 to USD 307 in 2021 and USD 416 in 2022.

Brief of 26 March 2025:

> Cereal production in 2024 is estimated at about 1.5 million tonnes, nearly three times higher than the drought-affected 2023 output, yet remaining about 6 percent below the five-year average.

Brief of 18 February 2026:

> Cereal production in 2025 is estimated at about 1.7 million tonnes, nearly 18 percent above the five-year average, reflecting improved weather conditions during the second half of the season. Although the season started with dry weather conditions between October 2024 and February 2025, above-average rainfall amounts between April and May boosted yields in key producing regions.

> Although local production has increased over the past two years, it covers about 60 percent of domestic annual needs and the country continues to rely on international markets to secure an adequate supply of wheat for local consumption.
resolvedSources.notes: The archive PDF was downloaded and converted with pdftotext; the extracts above are prose paragraphs, not tables. GIEWS revised its 2023 estimate from 302 000 t (Nov 2023) to 520 000 t (May 2024); both values are kept. GIEWS figures are FAO estimates built on its Country Cereal Balance Sheet, not Tunisian official statistics. Marketing year is July/June.

Production policy:

> To achieve the government's self-sufficiency goal of reaching average annual production of 3 MMT for cereals, of which 1.7 MMT is durum wheat, state-sponsored programs include:

> Tunisia's Office des Cereales (Cereal Board) maintains an official monopoly on the inventory, purchase, and sale of wheat and barley for the domestic market. resolvedSources.extracts:
Dated March 1, 2024. Sectoral context, para 8, p. 3:

> For the fourth consecutive year, below-average rainfall and extreme heat have combined to dramatically compromise Tunisia's grain production in 2022/23. As shown in Table 1 below, the Grain Board collected less than half of durum wheat quantities in 2023 compared to average drought years 2020-22 and two-thirds less than in a non-drought year (such as 2019), and almost no barley (1.3 percent of average drought years).

Table 1, "Grain quantities collected by OC (2019-2023)", '000 t, source Tunisia Grain Board (OC), rows (2019 / average 2020-2022 / 2023):

> Durum wheat 876.4 685.6 286.7
> Soft wheat 75.4 31.3 6.2
> Barley 332.9 39.5 0.5
> Total 1284.7 756.4 293.4

Para 8, p. 3 (continued):

> Consequently, average monthly grain import needs have skyrocketed (100,000 MT/month for durum wheat and 100,000 MT/month for barley, currently estimated at US$48 million/month for durum wheat and US$28 million/month for barley).

Footnote 15:

> This is particularly true in Tunisia where people remember vividly the bread riots that occurred from December 1983 to January 1984, triggered by a temporary rise in the price of bread due to the government austerity program.

Para 9, p. 3:

> For the period from July 2023 to June 2024, the Grain Board is facing an additional financing gap of around US$522 million due to very low local harvest of durum wheat and barley.

Footnote to Table 2, p. 4:

> Soft wheat import needs are not substantially impacted by drought since Tunisia is 95 percent dependent on imports.

Box 1, p. 4:

> The Grain Board (OC) is an SOE created in 1962 under the tutelage of Ministry of Agriculture, Water Resources and Fisheries (MAWRF) with a core mandate to regulate and ensure a stable supply of grain on the domestic market through domestic grain harvest collection, imports, and the management of strategic reserves.

> The OC has a de jure monopoly over grain trade (domestic collection and imports), except for barley (animal feed) for which domestic collection (traditionally) and imports (since April 2023) have been authorized for selected private operators.

> The OC buys grain domestically at farmgate prices fixed annually by a government decree. These prices have been below import-parity prices; they were increased by around 60 percent since 2022 to incentivize production.

> The OC sells the grain it purchases at subsidized prices to the millers who are granted specific acquisition quotas; the millers in turn sell the milled products (soft wheat bread flour, soft wheat pastry flour, durum semolina) to bakeries and processors similarly at subsidized prices under quota assignments. End products (such as bread, pasta, and couscous) are sold to consumers at subsidized prices.

> Because of CGC protracted payments, OC must resort to financing by the National Agriculture Bank which is difficult to mobilize and costly.

> CGC, a state-owned entity created in 1970, is responsible for providing compensatory payments to operators at the different segments of the grain value chain to cover the gap between market and administered prices.

Footnote 3:

> Farmgate gate prices in 2023 have been increased by 60.9 percent, 64.2 percent and 60.7 percent for durum wheat, soft wheat and barley respectively, compared to 2021. In February 2024, official farmgate prices for durum wheat and barley are respectively 3 percent sand 14 percent lower than OC import cost (Source OC).

Box 1 continued, p. 5:

> (iii) there are illegal and improper use of subsidized grain products, i.e., improper use of semolina for feed to animals, illegal leakages of grain products towards neighboring countries, as well as excessive consumption and wastage of bread and wheat-based products by end-consumers, e.g., wastage of 900,000 "baguettes" daily; and (iv) the system limits the active participation of the private sector

Para 10, p. 5:

> For calendar years 2022 and 2023, the OC was supposed to receive TND6,625 million (Tunisian Dinar) – i.e., approximately US$2,106 million - from the CGC, but funding effectively received from the compensation fund was only 38 percent (i.e., TND2,543 million or US$808 million).

> As of February 2024, the OC's estimated overall 2023 balance (yet to be audited) amounts to TND -900 million (equivalent to US$ -286 million) and OC's total debt to commercial banks is TND6,343 million (equivalent to US$2,016 million, out of which 83 percent towards the National Agriculture Bank - BNA).

Para 11, p. 5:

> the GoT is carrying out a series of measures that, if fully implemented, would lead to a more sustainable sector and sizeable budget savings in the range of US$400-600 million per year.

Para 10, p. 5 (continued):

> This situation makes it very difficult for OC to access additional financing from commercial banks for grain imports

Para 13:

> This series of reforms would lead to OC's budget and fiscal savings estimated at US$576 million per year

Table 3, "Summary reform measures of the grain value chain and associated savings", measure names (rows extracted as text; fiscal columns not used):

> 4 Strengthening of compensation for losses (FIDAC) [...] Approved (2024 Fiscal Law)- December 31, 2023
> 5 Improved access to seasonal credit for grain producers [...] Approved (2024 Fiscal Law)- December 31, 2023
> 9 Liberalization of soft wheat imports for industrial processing of pastry flour (PS-7) [...] Planned: Cabinet Council to review the draft Decision

Footnote 4 (to Table 3 measure "Strengthening of compensation for losses (FIDAC)", approved in the 2024 Fiscal Law):

> FIDAC (Fonds d'Indemnisation des Dommages Agricoles causés par les Calamités naturelles): is a farmers' compensation fund in case of natural disaster, including drought.

Results framework, p. 43:

> Food subsidy reform implementation plan prepared [...] Preparation of a reform plan for food subsidies and switch to cash transfer, including consultation and communication.

Footnote 17:

> 43.3 percent of bread subsidy for "Gros pain" and 43.5 percent of subsidy for other staple durum wheat-based products go to the poorest two quintiles of Tunisia households in 2022.

> Le blocage des prix et des salaires (1960-1970) : au cours de cette période, la politique de l'Etat en matière de prix à la production consistait en la fixation et le maintien des prix des produits agricoles à un niveau bas.

> La mise en place des subventions (1970-1984) : en 1971, la Caisse Générale de Compensation (CGC) est créée pour gérer un système de

English gloss: 1960-1970, the state fixed producer prices of agricultural products at a low level; 1970-1984, subsidies set up — in 1971 the CGC was created to manage a subsidy system.

PDF p. 33:

> Les seuls produits qui continuent après à être subventionnés sont les céréales d'alimentation humaine, l'huile

English gloss: after structural adjustment, the only products still subsidised are cereals for human consumption, (vegetable) oil [and others].

PDF p. 33 (citing INS 2013, analysis of the impact of food subsidies on poverty):

> qu'en 2010, seules 9,2 % des subventions sont orientées aux ménages les plus démunis, 60,5 % aux ménages de la classe moyenne, 7,5 % à la population aisée, alors que 22,8 % sont transférés hors ménages, notamment vers les entreprises de restauration hors foyer.

English gloss: in 2010 only 9.2% of subsidies went to the poorest households, 60.5% to middle-class households, 7.5% to the well-off, and 22.8% outside households, notably to out-of-home catering businesses.

PDF p. 52 (stability of access):

> Selon l'INC, le gaspillage du pain par les ménages a atteint les 900.000 pains/j, ce qui correspond à une valeur moyenne de l'ordre de 100 millions DT/an.

English gloss: according to the INC, household bread waste reached 900,000 loaves a day, worth about 100 million TND a year (no year given).

PDF p. 53:

> Le taux de dépendance vis-à-vis des céréales importées reste en moyenne de l'ordre de 60%, soit : • 40% pour le blé dur ; • 80% pour le blé tendre ; • 50% pour l'orge

English gloss: dependence on imported cereals averages about 60%: 40% durum wheat, 80% soft wheat, 50% barley.

PDF p. 54:

> La production céréalière connait une légère tendance à la baisse, malgré les investissements et les soutiens de l'Etat. [...] Elle est en grande partie issue des cultures pluviales (seulement 10% en irrigué) et reste soumise aux aléas climatiques.

> La moyenne se situe autour de 17 millions de Tonnes durant la période 2010-2018. Les rendements n'excèdent pas les 25 q/ha pour le blé dur, 21 q/ha pour le blé tendre et 16 q/ha pour l'orge avec une moyenne de 18q/ha pour la même période.

> La production de blé dur prédomine et progresse vu son adaptation aux conditions locales (+27% entre 2010-2018), contre un recul du blé tendre (-25%).

English gloss: cereal production shows a slight downward trend despite state investment and support; it is mostly rainfed (only 10% irrigated) and exposed to climate hazards. Average around "17 million tonnes" (sic) over 2010-2018. Yields do not exceed 25 q/ha durum, 21 q/ha soft wheat, 16 q/ha barley, average 18 q/ha. Durum production up 27% over 2010-2018, soft wheat down 25%.

PDF p. 55:

> La part de l'office des céréales dans la collecte physique a fortement diminué passant de 32% en 2005 à 2% en 2012, au profit d'opérateurs privés désormais majoritaires (58%) et des sociétés mutuelles de service agricoles (SMSA) (40%).

English gloss: OC's share of physical collection fell from 32% in 2005 to 2% in 2012, in favour of private operators (58%) and agricultural service cooperatives (40%).

PDF p. 116 (printed p. 114; page corrected by source-verifier, previously given as p. 121), trend micro-scenario (H1, "au fil de l'eau"), horizon 2035, V12-H1:

> La dépendance au marché international se poursuit pour les produits de base et les intrants (Taux de dépendance moyen des céréales 57% dont le Blé tendre avec 84%, le blé dur 41% et l'orge 51%)

PDF p. 108, footnote 94 to the same figures: (footnote text not found again by text search on re-check; page unconfirmed)

> Maintien de la moyenne des dix dernières années. Source : Observatoire Tunisien de l'Economie, 2023. Dépendance aux importations de blé.

English gloss: in the trend scenario to 2035, average cereal dependence stays at 57% (soft wheat 84%, durum 41%, barley 51%); the footnote says this is the ten-year average held constant (source Observatoire Tunisien de l'Economie, 2023).

### Livestock feed extracts (added for FND-TG-760/761)

PDF p. 55:

> sachant que la demande augmentera de 50% pour les céréales et doublera pour les aliments de bétail (SOLIDAR et PAM, 2020)

English gloss: by 2035 demand will rise 50% for cereals and double for livestock feed (citing SOLIDAR and WFP, 2020).

PDF p. 66 (section II.2.1.1 Disponibilité, Covid-19 and 2021-2022 shocks):

> les aliments de bétail, qui sont en grande partie importés (30% des besoins en graines de maïs, de blé fourrager, de tourteau de Soja et d'orge). La valeur des importations en 2021 a enregistré un accroissement significatif par rapport à 2019 (Fig. 1), soit 75% contre 26%. Ceci résulte essentiellement de l'accroissement des quantités importées, (surtout du tourteau de soja de 85% et de l'orge de 64%), mais aussi de la volatilité de leur prix sur le marché mondial (Fig. 2) et de la dévaluation du dinar tunisien. Les augmentations des prix ont atteint en 2021 un accroissement de 48% pour le maïs, 30% pour l'orge et 18% pour le soja.

English gloss: livestock feed is largely imported ("30% of needs" for maize, feed wheat, soybean meal and barley, as printed). The value of feed imports in 2021 rose 75% over 2019, mainly because of higher import volumes (soybean meal +85%, barley +64%), but also world price volatility and the devaluation of the Tunisian dinar. Prices rose in 2021 by 48% for maize, 30% for barley and 18% for soya.

> Vu l'augmentation drastique du cours de la matière première, les prix du concentré ont enregistré une hausse de 35% en 2022 par rapport à 2019. Il est prévu que la tendance haussière des prix du concentré va se poursuivre à un rythme plus rapide, ce qui constituera une menace sérieuse pour le secteur de l'élevage.

English gloss: concentrate feed prices rose 35% in 2022 compared with 2019; the upward trend is expected to continue faster, a serious threat to livestock farming.

> D'autres ont abandonné partiellement ou totalement leurs activités (tel le cas pour l'élevage avicole et laitier).

English gloss: some farmers partly or fully abandoned their activity (as in poultry and dairy farming).

PDF p. 66, Covid-19 and 2021-2022 shocks (continuation):

> D'autres ont abandonné partiellement ou totalement leurs activités (tel le cas pour l'élevage avicole et laitier).

English gloss: some poultry and dairy farmers partly or fully abandoned their activity in the context of the Covid-19 and input-price shocks; the study cites the IACE/UTAP 2021 survey.

PDF pp. 69-70 (2022 supply disruption):

> Concrètement, les chiffres montrent que c'est surtout l'orge qui a subi de fortes baisses à l'importation d'où l'explication, en partie, de l'indisponibilité temporaire de quantités suffisantes d'aliments de bétail qui a agi sur la disponibilité du lait et autres sources alimentaires de protéines animales.

> Au niveau du citoyen, ceci s'est ressenti sous forme de légères pénuries durant quelques semaines.

> L'opportunisme des intermédiaires et la spéculation de certains commerçants semblent avoir accentué cette crise temporaire.

English gloss: barley imports fell sharply (2022), partly explaining a temporary feed shortage affecting milk and other animal protein availability; consumers felt light shortages for a few weeks. Intermediary opportunism and some traders’ speculation appear to have worsened the crisis.
resolvedSources.notes: ITES is a state think tank attached to the Presidency; tier B. The 2010-2018 production sentence mixes units ("17 millions de Tonnes" is almost certainly quintals, i.e. about 1.7 Mt; elsewhere "26 MT" for 2009); it is quoted but not used as an indicator. The 2035 "projection" is a scenario assumption (ten-year average held constant), not a model. The CGC creation year here (1971) differs from the World Bank (1970, SRC-TG-705).

resolvedSources.title: The Unfinished Revolution: Bringing Opportunity, Good Jobs and Greater Wealth to All Tunisians — Chapter 9, Unleashing the Potential of Agriculture to Boost Growth in Interior Regions
resolvedSources.extracts:
Chapter subtitle, p. 259 (printed):

> Tunisia does not have an agricultural policy; rather it has a food security policy, which goes against the potential of its agricultural sector

Box 9.1 discussion, pp. 261-262:

> not have a strong comparative advantage in cereals, which are intensive in land and are socially less profitable than arboriculture, fruits, and vegetables (box 9.1).

> Tunisia is also competitive in durum wheat (rain-fed and irrigated) and was also competitive in irrigated soft wheat when the international prices spiked in 2008, such that temporarily it became profitable to produce soft wheat in Tunisia. The competitiveness in soft wheat is limited to the irrigated areas and areas in the north and northwest regions where the rainfall is more favorable (not shown).

Section 9.2, p. 263:

> Market price support is carried out mostly through the implementation of a guaranteed minimum price for producers of cereals and intervention purchases carried out by the state marketing boards for milk, sugar beet, and tobacco.

> Cereals (soft wheat, durum wheat, and barley) account for a further third of the expenditure on market price support.

p. 265:

> pays inadequate quality bonuses for cereals, and caps the prices of processed foods.

p. 266:

> In 2009 the budgetary cost of food subsidies was approximately 1.5 percent of GDP, and this amount increased to over three percent of GDP in 2012 (table 9.3).

pp. 267-268:

> it is estimated that the annual cost of protecting employment in the cereals sector is four times the national per capita income.

> The farms that would lose from liberalization are generally those that produce cereals in the better--watered north and northwest parts of the country.

> contrary to popular belief, the agricultural policy does not promote small family farms but mostly benefits a few large land owners (producing wheat, milk, and beef), who are often the most prosperous. This is because most support is provided based on output and farm size.

Additional extracts on Mediterranean and export crops (added for FND-TG-860/861). Page numbers follow the printed page footers, checked page by page:

Chapter introduction, p. 260:

> The current system of state intervention has repressed the agricultural sector, distorting production away from Mediterranean products in which Tunisia has a natural comparative advantage toward continental products in which Tunisia is not very competitive but which are key to food security.

p. 262:

> Tunisia is very competitive in production of olive oil and tomatoes (as shown by the DRC < 1) in each of the three years for which the analysis has been carried out (2000, 2004, and 2008). It is also competitive in production of oranges and potatoes, except in 2008 when the price of fertilizer was extremely high.

p. 262:

> The most competitive products, namely durum wheat, arboriculture (including fruit and olive oil), vegetables, and fisheries--which represent 58 percent of production over the last 20 years--contribute to the growth of the sector only up to about 46 percent, while non-competitive products (cereals, excluding durum wheat, beef, milk)--which concern 39 percent of production--contributed up to about 52 percent (table 9.1).

> in 1998 Tunisia used only approximately 55 percent of its citrus export quota (CNEA 2005b), and this amount was still only approximately 60 percent in 2010 and 2011

p. 263:

> Similarly, Tunisian used only 25 percent of its tomato quota in 1998 and still used only 50 to 70 percent of its quota in 2010 and 2011, respectively. Even for olive oil, Tunisia still manages to export only about 20 percent of its quota.

> For other products, such as tomatoes, the shortfalls in taking advantage of these export opportunities is also due to the fact that the EU import quotas are subject to specific calendars which further restrict their use.

Box 9.2, p. 264:

> Citrus production has stagnated for more than a decade, and growing domestic demand absorbs more than 90 percent of local production. Current citrus exports to the EU amount to 24,000 tons and represent only 60 percent of the country's preferential quota.

Table 9.2, p. 265, "Exports to the EU for Selected Products under Quota, 2010 and 2011" (tons 2010 | 2011 | EU quota | % of quota 2010 | 2011; source Tunisia Ministry of Agriculture):

> Citrus fruit 24580 23610 39355 62 60

> Tomatoes 9820 13384 18816 52 71

> Olive oil (conditioned) 10877 12035 56000 19 21

pp. 265-266:

> The focus of farmers on products in which Tunisia is not competitive is the direct result of existing agricultural policies. In fact much of the growth in agriculture has been driven by subsidies and the trade protection of products in which Tunisia is not competitive.

> In 2008-2009, the largest share was allocated to fuel subsides (approximately 40 percent of total input subsidies), milk collection premia (approximately 40 percent), and irrigation subsidies (approximately 18 percent).

pp. 268-269:

> The bias introduced by protection of selected agricultural products results in a reallocation of capital and labor toward those overprotected products at the expense of alternative products in which Tunisia's exports have a comparative advantage, thus introducing an anti-export bias.

> Existing policies are strongly targeted toward supporting continental products (that is, they are largely focused on supporting cereals, milk, and beef), implicitly discriminating against Mediterranean products.

Additional extracts on the support framework, budget transfers and simulations (added for FND-TG-920/921/922). Page numbers here follow the printed page footers of the PDF (the footer number closes each page), which may differ by one or two from the page references above:

Chapter opening (p. 260):

> This chapter suggests that Tunisia does not really have an agricultural policy but has instead a food security policy that in fact hinders the development of its agricultural sector. The current system of state intervention has repressed the agricultural sector, distorting production away from Mediterranean products in which Tunisia has a natural comparative advantage toward continental products in which Tunisia is not very competitive but which are key to food security.

Section 9.2, p. 265:

> Agricultural production increased by 67 percent (in value) over the period 1990-2010, but almost one-third (17 percent of the value) originates in bovine beef and milk, in which Tunisia is not competitive.

p. 265:

> Market price support is significant, accounting for over 30 percent of total budgetary transfers to agriculture in recent years [...] Market price support is carried out mostly through the implementation of a guaranteed minimum price for producers of cereals and intervention purchases carried out by the state marketing boards for milk, sugar beet, and tobacco. [...] Market price support is particularly important in the milk sector, which accounts for over 50 percent of expenditure on market price support in recent years. Cereals (soft wheat, durum wheat, and barley) account for a further third of the expenditure on market price support.

p. 266:

> The simple average of the "most favored nation" (MFN) rates applied to agri-food products is 24.6 percent (compared to 16.5 percent for all products), with a maximum rate of 36 percent. "Record prices" (those above 15 percent, according to the World Trade Organization [WTO] definition) account for about 60.5 percent of agricultural tariff lines, compared to 32.5 percent for non-agricultural products.

> Input subsidies (such as improved seeds, forage seeds, energy, irrigation water, and so on) also play an important role and account for approximately 20 to 25 percent of total budgetary transfers in recent years: In 2008-2009, the largest share was allocated to fuel subsides (approximately 40 percent of total input subsidies), milk collection premia (approximately 40 percent), and irrigation subsidies (approximately 18 percent). Fertilizer subsidies were discontinued in 1991.

> the state controls the margins of retail sales of several products, puts pressure on wholesalers to keep their prices low, imports when prices are rising (including for products like vegetables for which there is no guaranteed price), pays inadequate quality bonuses for cereals, and caps the prices of processed foods.

> The budgetary direct costs of policies reached approximately 0.8 percent of GDP in 2010 (or TND 350 million) [...] although Tunisia committed (in the framework of the 1994 Uruguay Round of trade negotiations) to reduce the overall mass of domestic support (from 76 million to 66 million dollars), in fact the budget expenditure for agricultural support has been steadily increasing [...] Between 2000 and 2009 the share of market price support and input subsidies increased from 31 to 53 percent while those of investment aid [...] and those intended for general services actually decreased

p. 267:

> the World Bank estimates that the net effect of trade protection of agricultural goods is equivalent to a loss of approximately four percent of consumer spending if the consumer purchases remain constant, and approximately 5.6 percent if consumers readjust their spending in response to changes in relative prices (table 9.4) (for a full discussion of the model and these results see World Bank 2006)

> the elimination of tariff barriers on agricultural products would increase GDP by approximately 0.8 percent [...] However, the elimination of tariff barriers on agricultural goods would also cause a loss of approximately 87,000 jobs from agriculture that would have to be absorbed by other sectors.

Table 9.4 (p. 268), "Effects on the Entire Economy of Opening Up Trade in Agricultural Goods", source CGE model simulations, World Bank (2006). Rows (baseline / full liberalisation with EU agricultural subsidies / without EU agricultural subsidies):

> Economic growth (% per year, in the years following liberalization) 5.7 / 6.5 / 6.2
> Labor force transferred to other sectors (in thousand jobs) - / 87 / 67
> Gains of adjustment (million TND through 2025) - / 7107 / 4441

p. 268:

> Using a linear programming model [...] the World Bank estimates that nearly 70 percent of farms would gain from the removal of price distortions in the agricultural sector (table 9.5). [...] The farms that would lose from liberalization are generally those that produce cereals in the better-watered north and northwest parts of the country.

p. 269:

> contrary to popular belief, the agricultural policy does not promote small family farms but mostly benefits a few large land owners (producing wheat, milk, and beef), who are often the most prosperous. This is because most support is provided based on output and farm size.

> Agricultural producers who operate in filieres (sectors) that hold great promise (for example, dried fruit, olive oil, fruit, and vegetables), prevalently in interior regions, often receive little or no support from agricultural policies and have great difficulty in accessing financing, inputs, information, or advice

Box 9.3 (p. 270), farmer testimony:

> despite the recognized quality of its olive oil, Tunisia is still using only 20 percent of its quota of exports to the European Union.

Recommendations section (pp. 273-274):

> (a) Progressively shift away from price support and orient agricultural policy toward direct income support

> Taking action to improve access to finance for the agricultural sector. Access to finance is especially challenging for investments in arboriculture (olive oil and fruit), which entail several years between the initial investment and the start of the production phase.
resolvedSources.notes: Chapter of the World Bank Development Policy Review published in 2014; underlying analyses date from 2006-2012 (CGE model World Bank 2006; DRC analysis World Bank 2009 using 2000, 2004, 2008 prices). Its view that cereal producers receive market price support contrasts with the 2024 World Bank statement that farmgate prices were below import parity (SRC-TG-705); the two describe different periods and price contexts. The DRC table extracted with shifted values and is not quoted; only prose is used.

resolvedSources.title: INC : 113 mille tonnes par an de pain gaspillées par les ménages
resolvedSources.extracts:
Article of 25 May 2017 reporting an INC presentation:

> Présentés aujourd'hui par Tarek Ben Jazia, Directeur général de l'INC, les principaux résultats de ces enquêtes et sondages, réalisés durant les mois de mai et juin 2016, ont démontré que 71,3% des personnes sondées affirment que le niveau de gaspillage en Tunisie est élevé.

> Ainsi, le pain et les produits céréaliers accaparent la part du lion du gaspillage chez les ménages, avec respectivement 15,7% et 10,2% contre 2,3% des produits laitiers.

> En valeur, la moyenne du gaspillage alimentaire par ménage par mois est estimée à 17 dinars, soit 5% des dépenses alimentaires.

> L'INC a dévoilé que les principales sources de gaspillage alimentaire se résument principalement dans l'achat excessif avec 87,9%%, la préparation excessive par rapport aux besoins avec 87,3% et les achats non planifiés avec 84%.

> Au volet de la consommation du pain en Tunisie, l'INC a dévoilé qu'en 2014, les estimations tablent autour de 900 000 pains jetés quotidiennement pour un coût évalué à 300 000 dinars, soit l'équivalent de 102 mille tonnes et de 100 millions de dinars par an.

> Les résultats des enquêtes récentes ont démontré que le reste du pain non consommé par ménage par an représente 42 kg pour un total de 113 mille tonnes par an.

> Le gaspillage du pain est de plus en plus élevé en Tunisie, et ce, malgré le fait que 73% des personnes enquêtées précisent que le niveau actuel des prix du pain n'encourage pas à en acheter plus que de besoin.

> Dans le même sillage, 44% des interrogés ont indiqué que la qualité du pain subventionné est bonne, contre 43% de qualité moyenne et 13% de mauvaise qualité. Sachant que 2% uniquement des Tunisiens connaissent la vraie valeur de la subvention allouée au Grand pain et 1% pour la Baguette. Sachant également que 400 millions de dinars correspondent au montant alloué pour subventionner à l'année la farine de pain.

> Pendant le mois de Ramadan, le gaspillage alimentaire augmente. D'ailleurs, 66,6% des personnes sondées ont dévoilé que les plats cuisinés se taillent la part du lion du gaspillage. Suivent le pain avec 46%, les fruits avec 31,7%

Reference box: "Sur un total de 2,7 millions de ménages à fin 2015 ... Pain : 73kg; Baguettes : 105 pièces; Gros pains : 112 pièces."

English gloss: INC surveys of May-June 2016. Households waste 15.7% of bread and 10.2% of cereal products (2.3% of dairy). Average waste is 17 dinars per household per month, 5% of food spending. Main self-reported causes: over-buying (87.9%), over-cooking (87.3%), unplanned purchases (84%). An INC 2014 estimate put bread thrown away at 900,000 loaves a day (300,000 dinars a day), equal to 102 thousand tonnes and 100 MD a year; recent surveys give 42 kg per household per year, 113 thousand tonnes in total. 73% of respondents say the current bread price does not encourage buying more than needed. 44% rate subsidised bread quality good, 43% average, 13% poor; 2% know the real subsidy on "gros pain", 1% on the baguette; 400 MD a year subsidises bread flour. In Ramadan, 66.6% of respondents name cooked dishes as the most wasted item, 46% name bread (shares of respondents, not waste rates).
resolvedSources.notes:
- Press report of an INC presentation; the INC survey report itself was not available (inc.nat.tn had an expired TLS certificate). Sample size not given.
- The 900,000 loaves per day figure is an INC estimate for 2014. It is repeated unchanged by the FAO/ministry study around 2017 (SRC-TG-901) and in 2026 press (SRC-TG-910), so later dates are restatements, not new measurements.

relatedItems.title: Tunisia imports more than half of its cereals (about 60% on ITES averages) and almost all of its soft (bread) wheat, even in good harvest years
Rainfed cereal output swings with rainfall and collapsed in the 2023 drought, cutting the harvest by roughly two-thirds or more

Households throw away about a sixth of the bread they buy; the World Bank names the universal cereal price subsidy as a driver and the FAO lists it as a possible cause, though household surveys find little direct price effect
